cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Ferrous metals contain iron; cast iron, low-carbon steel, high-carbon steel and stainless steel are the main ferrous materials.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Non-ferrous metals include aluminium, copper, brass, bronze, zinc and lead; they do not contain iron and generally resist corrosion better.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Alloying alters properties: adding carbon to iron increases hardness and strength; chromium adds corrosion resistance (stainless steel).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Heat treatment changes material properties: annealing softens, hardening increases strength, quenching locks in a hard structure, temperpering reduces brittleness.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Cold working (work hardening) increases strength and hardness by deforming the metal at room temperature but reduces ductility.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Carbon content in steel is critical: low carbon (0.1-0.3%) is ductile and weldable; high carbon (0.6-1.4%) is hard and wear-resistant.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Aluminium is lightweight, corrosion-resistant and an excellent conductor; widely used in aerospace and transport engineering.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Copper has excellent electrical and thermal conductivity; used for wiring, heat exchangers and plumbing.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Brass (copper + zinc) is corrosion-resistant and machinable; used for valves, fittings and decorative components.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Bronze (copper + tin) is hard, wear-resistant and corrosion-resistant; used for bearings, marine fittings and sculptures.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Material selection depends on required properties, cost, availability, manufacturability and environmental impact.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Metals & Alloys
cards.back: Stainless steel resists corrosion due to a chromium oxide layer; used in chemical, medical and food-processing applications.

cards.front: What should you know about gcse engineering exam tips — metals & alloys?
cards.back: 1. For Metals & Alloys questions, use precise design and technology terminology 2. Consider function, aesthetics, ergonomics, sustainability and cost in your answers 3. When evaluating, justify your design decisions with reference to user needs and specifications 4. Show your understanding of Metals & Alloys through both theory and practical application 5. Reference real products and manufacturing processes where relevant
